title: NPT, CTBT, NSG and the Civil Nuclear Deal

cards.h: Outside the club, but inside the trade
cards.b:
India never signed the NPT or the CTBT. Yet since 2008 it can trade in nuclear fuel and technology, thanks to the NSG waiver and the India–US civil nuclear deal. It has also joined three of the four export-control regimes.

UPSC asks why India rejects the NPT and CTBT, how the 2008 deal changed things, and why NSG membership is still blocked.

The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. It recognises five nuclear weapon states: those that tested before 1 January 1967 (US, USSR/Russia, UK, France, China). Everyone else must stay non-nuclear.

  • Article VI asks the nuclear states to pursue disarmament in good faith, but sets no deadline.
  • Article X allows withdrawal (North Korea, 2003).

India calls the NPT discriminatory: it divides the world into nuclear 'haves' and 'have-nots' for ever. Jaswant Singh called this 'nuclear apartheid' in 1998. India says it will not join as a non-nuclear state.

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1996. It bans all nuclear explosions. It is not in force, because it needs all 44 states listed in Annex 2 (those with nuclear reactors) to ratify. India, Pakistan and North Korea have not signed; the US and China have signed but not ratified.

India blocked the text at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva in 1996. Its reasons: no time-bound disarmament, and the entry-into-force clause forced India's hand. India keeps a voluntary moratorium on tests since 1998.

NSG (1974–75)

48 members who control nuclear exports. India is not a member.

MTCR

Missile Technology Control Regime. India joined in June 2016.

Wassenaar Arrangement

Conventional arms and dual-use goods. India joined in December 2017.

Australia Group

Chemical and biological controls. India joined in January 2018.

India's domestic law: the WMD Act (2005), which bans transfers to non-state actors, in line with UNSC Resolution 1540 (2004).

India separated its reactors into civilian (under IAEA safeguards) and military (outside). It promised to keep its test moratorium and strong export controls. In return it received a clean waiver from NSG rules, the only non-NPT state to get one.

cards.h: What the deal gave India, and what it did not
cards.b:
• Gains: imported uranium from Russia, Kazakhstan, Canada, Australia, Uzbekistan and France; deals with France, the US and Japan (2016); recognition as a responsible nuclear state; the end of decades of 'technology denial'.
  • Limits: no new US reactor was built for years, mainly because of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (2010), which let operators claim against suppliers (Section 17(b)). Foreign suppliers feared unlimited liability.
  • 2025 change: the SHANTI Act (December 2025) replaced the 2010 liability law and the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. It caps operator liability, removes the supplier liability that blocked foreign firms, and lets private companies operate plants under licence. Critics say it shifts risk to taxpayers.

India ratified the Convention on Supplementary Compensation (CSC) in 2016.

India applied for NSG membership in 2016. At the Seoul plenary (June 2016), China led opposition, saying non-NPT states need a common, criteria-based approach. That would also bring in Pakistan, which India and many members oppose because of the A.Q. Khan network.

Membership requires consensus, so one state can block. As of 2026 India is still outside. In practice the 2008 waiver gives most of the trade benefits; membership would give a voice in making rules.

Non-proliferation purists say the 2008 deal rewarded a state that stayed out of the NPT. Supporters reply that bringing India into the system is better than isolating it. India also backs the FMCT (fissile material cut-off) talks in principle but did not sign the 2017 Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

• Rajiv Gandhi Action Plan (1988) at the UN: a timebound plan to eliminate nuclear weapons by 2010.
  • India supports a Nuclear Weapons Convention and a universal, non-discriminatory approach.
  • India–Pakistan CBMs: the 1988 agreement on not attacking nuclear facilities (lists exchanged each 1 January) and the 2005 missile-test notification.
  • Energy goal: 100 GW nuclear power by 2047, small modular reactors and private entry under the SHANTI Act.
